windows.focusPhrase: This is one reason varnish thickness fails to provide a dependable age. Biological hypotheses are tested by locating cells, pigments or molecular traces within intact layers, not merely by finding microbes on an exposed surface.
windows.recognizedPhrase: This is one reason varnish thickness fails to provide a dependable age. Biological hypotheses are tested by locating cells, pigments or molecular traces within intact layers, not merely by finding microbes on an exposed surface.

windows.focusPhrase: Researchers therefore combine microscopic, chemical and environmental evidence. They compare texture, elemental composition, slope, exposure and nearby dust sources. A dark patch on a sheltered face may not have the same history as a visually similar patch exposed to wind. Equally, a newly detached flake may reveal an uncoated surface beneath an older layer. Dating attempts sometimes compare varnish with independently dated rock surfaces, but the relationship is rarely linear. A stable surface can experience pulses of deposition separated by erosion or inactivity. The useful question is often whether a coating predates or postdates a known event, not its exact calendar age.

windows.focusPhrase: The safest conclusion is not that one process is always dominant, but that several interacting processes must be evaluated together. Varnish can preserve useful environmental signals, yet those signals are filtered by the stability and history of the surface. Interpretation becomes stronger when it explains both coated and uncoated areas, rather than selecting only the most dramatic example. Good sampling is deliberately comparative. Investigators take material from different orientations and include bare controls, then document precisely where each fragment came from. Because removal is destructive and cultural sites may be protected, analytical methods increasingly aim to obtain more information from smaller samples.
